title: Base Rates: Start With How Common
objective: After this level you can explain why you should start with how common something is before judging a single case.
summary: The base rate is how common something is in the whole population. Start there before judging one case: when you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras.

cards.headline: You hear hoofbeats outside. Horse or zebra?
cards.body: Unless you live next to a zoo, you guess horse. Doctors have a saying built on exactly that hunch, and it holds one of the most useful ideas in this chapter.

cards.headline: Think horses, not zebras
cards.body: "When you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras." The saying is usually credited to Theodore Woodward of the University of Maryland School of Medicine, who reportedly used a version of it from the 1940s. It reminds doctors that a common explanation is far likelier than a rare one. "Zebra" even became medical slang for a surprising, rare diagnosis.

cards.headline: The base rate: how common, before any clue
cards.body: The share of people in a whole population who have something is its prevalence, or base rate. It can be given as a percent, or per 10,000 or 100,000 people. It is where you start: before you judge any one case, ask how common the thing is to begin with.

cards.fact: A clue that fits both explanations can't beat a big base-rate gap.
cards.context: Picture a made-up town of 10,000 people. This week 1,000 have a cold and 1 has a rare illness, and both cause a cough. Among people coughing, colds outnumber the rare illness 1,000 to 1. That is why test results and other clues are read against how common a condition is. Horses first.

cards.headline: Base rates: set
learned: Base rate = how common in the whole population
Start with the base rate before any clue
A shared clue can't beat a big base-rate gap

options.label: The rate at which a test gives wrong answers
options.rationale: That describes a test's errors, not how common something is.

options.label: How fast a disease spreads between people
options.rationale: Spread is a different measure; a base rate is a share of the population.

options.label: How common something is in the whole population
The lowest risk any one person can have
options.rationale: It is a share of a population, not a minimum.

questions.explanation: The base rate, or prevalence, is the share of a whole population who have something: the place to start.

questions.prompt: Why do doctors say "think horses, not zebras"?

options.label: Rare diseases can never be diagnosed
options.rationale: Rare diagnoses are real; they are just less likely.

options.label: A common cause is far likelier than a rare one
Zebras are hard to tell apart from horses
options.rationale: It is about how common things are, not how they look.

options.label: Common illnesses are always more dangerous
options.rationale: The saying is about likelihood, not danger.

questions.explanation: When a clue fits both a common and a rare cause, the common one is usually the answer, because it is so much more frequent.

questions.prompt: Like Level 6's rates, a base rate is often given per 100,000 people. What does that let you see that a total can't?

options.label: How common it is, person for person
Exactly who in the population has it
options.rationale: A rate describes a whole group, not individuals.

options.label: How many people will have it next year
options.rationale: A base rate describes now; it isn't a forecast.

options.label: Whether a test for it is accurate
options.rationale: How accurate a test is is a separate question.

questions.explanation: Dividing by the population puts places of any size on one scale: how common something is for each person.
